subtitle: Back up your data — and schedule it

intro.html: A backup is the one privacy and security step that protects you from everything: a stolen laptop, a dead drive, ransomware, a hacked account or a coffee spill. This walkthrough shows what to back up, how to do it on each device with tools you already have, how to keep backups encrypted, and how to make them run on a schedule so you never have to remember.

subsections.title: The 3-2-1 Rule
subsections.summary: Three copies, two kinds of storage, one far away.

items.title: 3 copies
items.html: Your original plus two backups. One backup can fail; two rarely fail at the same time.

items.title: 2 kinds of storage
items.html: For example your laptop’s drive and an external drive — so one fault or one bad batch of disks can’t take out everything.

items.title: 1 copy somewhere else
items.html: Offsite: an encrypted cloud backup, or a drive kept at a friend’s or at work. A fire or burglary takes everything in one place.

blocks.label: Sync is not a backup
blocks.html: iCloud Drive, Google Drive, Dropbox and OneDrive sync: delete or encrypt a file by accident (or by ransomware) and the change copies everywhere. A backup keeps older versions you can go back to.

subsections.title: What to Back Up
subsections.summary: The things you can’t download again.

items.details: Usually the most irreplaceable thing people own. Include your phone’s camera roll.

items.text: Your password manager vault (exported, encrypted) and 2FA backup codes
items.details: Losing these can lock you out of everything. Keep an encrypted export, and print backup codes for your most important accounts.
Use your provider’s export, or a desktop mail app such as Thunderbird that keeps a local copy.
Signal and WhatsApp have their own backup or transfer options — check them before changing phones.

items.text: Exports from accounts you rely on
items.details: Google Takeout, Apple’s Data & Privacy page and most social networks let you download your data.

blocks.html: Apps and the operating system can be reinstalled, so they matter less — but a full system backup (like Time Machine) makes restoring a broken computer much faster.

subsections.title: Back Up Your Computer
subsections.summary: Built-in tools for Mac, Windows and Linux.

blocks.html: You need an external drive at least as big as the data you’re backing up (twice as big is better, so it can keep older versions). Plug it in and follow the steps for your system.

items.title: Mac: Time Machine
items.text: System Settings → General → Time Machine → Add Backup Disk, pick your drive and tick Encrypt Backup. Time Machine then backs up automatically every hour while the drive is connected, and keeps hourly, daily and weekly versions. Under Options you can change the frequency. Apple’s guide.

items.title: Windows: File History
items.text:
Control Panel → System and Security → File History → select your drive → Turn on. Under Advanced settings choose how often to save copies (every hour by default) and how long to keep them. Encrypt the drive with BitLocker if your edition of Windows has it. Microsoft’s guide.

The newer “Windows Backup” app backs up to OneDrive, which isn’t end-to-end encrypted.

items.title: Linux: Déjà Dup (Backups)
items.text: Install Déjà Dup (called “Backups” on many systems), choose the folders and your drive, keep Encrypt backup on with a strong password, and turn on Back Up Automatically. For the system itself, Timeshift takes snapshots you can roll back to after a bad update.

items.title: iPhone: encrypted backup to your computer
items.text: Connect the iPhone to a Mac (Finder) or a Windows PC (the Apple Devices app). Select the phone, choose Back up all the data on your iPhone to this computer and tick Encrypt local backup — that also saves passwords, Health and Wi-Fi data. Store the password in your password manager. Apple’s guide · about encrypted backups.

items.title: iPhone: iCloud Backup
items.text: Settings → your name → iCloud → iCloud Backup. It runs automatically each night while charging on Wi-Fi. Turn on Advanced Data Protection (see De-Apple Yourself) so Apple can’t read it.

items.title: Android: built-in backup
items.text: Settings → System → Backup. Most phones back up to your Google account; on GrapheneOS and CalyxOS, Seedvault backs up to a USB drive or your own cloud instead. Photos are better handled by an encrypted photo app — see photo alternatives.

items.title: Any phone: copy photos to your computer
items.text: Every few weeks, copy the camera roll to your computer, where your computer backup picks it up. Or use an encrypted photo service like ente, or a self-hosted one like Immich.

subsections.title: Encrypted Backup Apps
subsections.summary: Cross-platform tools that encrypt before uploading.

blocks.html: These encrypt everything on your device before it’s copied, so the drive or cloud you back up to only ever sees scrambled data. They also deduplicate, so keeping many versions takes little extra space.

items.label: Kopia
items.desc: Easy desktop app or command line, with scheduling built in. Backs up to drives or almost any cloud.

items.label: Duplicati
items.desc: Web-based app with a scheduler, encrypting to drives and many cloud services.

items.label: restic
items.desc: Fast, reliable command-line backups; great with a schedule (see below).

items.label: BorgBackup + Vorta
items.desc: Borg is a mature, efficient backup engine; Vorta gives it a friendly app and scheduler.

items.label: Déjà Dup
items.desc: Simple encrypted backups with automatic scheduling.

items.label: Cryptomator
items.desc: Encrypts a folder before your cloud syncs it — for files you keep in any cloud.

blocks.text: Where to keep the offsite copy

blocks.html: Any of the encrypted cloud storage services, a cheap storage host used with Kopia, restic or Borg (they encrypt, so the host can’t see your files), or a second drive you keep at someone else’s home.

subsections.title: Schedule Automatic Backups
subsections.summary: Set it once so you never have to remember.

blocks.html: The backup that runs on its own is the one that actually happens. Time Machine, File History, Déjà Dup, Kopia, Duplicati and Vorta all have a schedule setting — turn it on and pick daily (or hourly). If you use restic on the command line, schedule it yourself:

blocks.code:
# create an encrypted repository on your backup drive
restic -r /Volumes/Backup/restic init

# save the repository password where only you can read it
echo 'your-long-repository-password' > ~/.restic-pass
chmod 600 ~/.restic-pass

# run a first backup
restic -r /Volumes/Backup/restic --password-file ~/.restic-pass backup ~/Documents ~/Pictures
blocks.label: Run in a terminal (macOS or Linux)

blocks.code:
# open your schedule
crontab -e

# add this line: back up every day at 02:00, then keep 7 daily, 4 weekly and 12 monthly versions
0 2 * * * restic -r /Volumes/Backup/restic --password-file $HOME/.restic-pass backup $HOME/Documents $HOME/Pictures --quiet && restic -r /Volumes/Backup/restic --password-file $HOME/.restic-pass forget --keep-daily 7 --keep-weekly 4 --keep-monthly 12 --prune --quiet
blocks.label: crontab

blocks.text: 2b. Or a systemd timer (Linux) — runs even if the computer was off at 02:00

blocks.code:
# ~/.config/systemd/user/backup.service
[Unit]
Description=restic backup

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/bin/restic -r /mnt/backup/restic --password-file %h/.restic-pass backup %h/Documents %h/Pictures

# ~/.config/systemd/user/backup.timer
[Unit]
Description=Daily restic backup

[Timer]
OnCalendar=daily
Persistent=true

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target
blocks.label: Two small files

blocks.code:
systemctl --user daemon-reload
systemctl --user enable --now backup.timer
systemctl --user list-timers   # check when it runs next
blocks.label: Turn the timer on

blocks.html: Open Task Scheduler → Create Basic Task → name it “Backup” → Daily → pick a time → Start a program, and point it at your backup app’s command (for example restic.exe with the same arguments as above). Tick “Run task as soon as possible after a scheduled start is missed” in the task’s settings.

blocks.label: Tip
blocks.html: A schedule only helps if the drive is there. If you use an external drive, plug it in at the same time every week — or back up to a network drive or the cloud, which is always connected.

subsections.title: Test Your Restore
subsections.summary: A backup you’ve never restored is a guess.

items.text: Restore one file into a new folder and open it
items.details: restic: restic -r /Volumes/Backup/restic --password-file ~/.restic-pass restore latest --target ~/restore-test. Time Machine: open the folder in Finder and choose “Browse Time Machine Backups”.

items.text: Check the last backup date every month
items.details: restic: restic snapshots. Time Machine and File History show the date of the last backup in their settings.

items.text: Keep the backup password somewhere you’ll have without the computer
items.details: In your password manager and on paper in a safe place. An encrypted backup without its password is gone for good.

items.text: Make sure the offsite copy works too
items.details: Try restoring something from the cloud copy, not just the drive on your desk.
